item.title: @convequity：分析机构认为Fractile芯片在内存速度与容量指标上难以兼得
item.description:
We think Fractile is unlikely to deliver both the memory speed and the memory capacity it claims on the same chip.

Fractile's headline claim is about 25x the per-chip bandwidth of HBM-based GPUs and XPUs, while keeping the model in cheaper, larger-capacity DRAM instead of HBM.

Bandwidth is how fast data moves between the memory and the processor. Capacity is how much data the memory stores.

The two come from different parts of the design. Bandwidth comes from stacking DRAM directly on the logic die, the chip that does the computing. Capacity depends on how many DRAM dies are in that stack.

If Fractile stacks only 2 to 4 DRAM dies on the logic die, it cannot match HBM-based chips on capacity in a like-for-like comparison. A stack that short limits how much memory each chip holds.

d-Matrix's Raptor shows the trade in practice. Raptor has 32GB of 3D DRAM per card. HBM4 accelerators have 192 to 288GB. d-Matrix plans to make up the capacity at rack scale.

The exception is a fan-out architecture, which spreads memory sideways across the package rather than relying purely on stacked dies.

Our view is that with a stack of only 2 to 4 DRAM dies, Fractile cannot match HBM-based chips on capacity per chip. The two things to watch are how many DRAM dies Fractile stacks and whether it uses a fan-out design.

Deeper dive available at Convequity.

item.title: @convequity：专家数据成本与模型蒸馏技术对中美顶尖AI实验室竞争格局的影响分析
item.description:
We think expensive expert data explains part of the lead Anthropic's Opus and OpenAI's Astra hold over Chinese models. Distillation lets rivals copy some of that ability at a fraction of the cost, making the lead harder to defend.

Both labs pay top specialists for their knowledge and judgment, up to $500 for a single conversation. We see only one Chinese lab paying at that level, and the leading Chinese labs spend less.

In distillation, a weaker model learns from a stronger model's answers.

In our illustration, a lab pays experts $400 an hour for 10,000 hours. That is $4 million of training data.

The lab sells the resulting model at $40 per equivalent hour. It earns back the $4 million in gross revenue after 100,000 hours.

A rival then buys 10,000 hours of the model's output at the same $40 an hour. That costs $400,000, a tenth of the original cost, and the rival captures much of the same ability.

Chinese teams say this works on some tasks and does not yet produce a full copy.

A frontier lab can protect the edge by selling its best systems only to a small group of U.S. enterprises. Once those capabilities go on wider sale, distillation lets some of the knowledge leak out. The thing to watch is when each lab puts its best system on wider sale.

Our view is that the expensive first wave from proprietary labs pays for the breakthrough. A cheaper second wave, with Chinese models in it, then brings it to far more people.

item.title: @convequity：Convequity：超大规模云厂商投资回报率与企业价值倍数分析，估值修复空间较大
item.description:
ROIC / WACC vs EV / IC: Hyperscalers Marked Down Too Far. Neo-Clouds, Mostly Not.

Convequity's AI Bubble Barometer (ABBX) pairs two metrics on its Fundamentals tab:

ROIC / WACC Ratio: return on AI capital (ROIC) over the cost of that capital (WACC). Above 1x, the spending creates value.

EV / IC Multiple: enterprise value over invested capital, what the market pays per dollar of capital.

Our question: has EV / IC fallen more than ROIC / WACC justifies?

1. HYPERSCALERS ($MSFT $AMZN $GOOGL $META $ORCL $CRWV $SPCX)

- ROIC / WACC fell 6%, from 2.82x (2Q26 reading) to 2.65x (3Q26 reading, live since 13 Nov).
- EV / IC fell 24%, from 6.80x at the 9 Oct close to 5.15x at the 25 Nov close.

EV / IC fell about four times as much, with ROIC / WACC still at a respectable 2.65x.

Clearest case, Google: EV / IC fell from 6.35x to 4.59x over the same closes; its ROIC / WACC edged up from 2.31x (2Q26) to 2.32x (3Q26).

2. NEO-CLOUDS ($NBIS $IREN $APLD $CORZ $CIFR $BTDR)

- ROIC / WACC fell 20%, from 1.40x (2Q26) to 1.12x (3Q26).
- EV / IC fell 57%, from 3.18x at the 9 Oct close to 1.38x at the 25 Nov close.

EV / IC fell faster here too, but mostly for good reason: at 1.12x, ROIC / WACC barely clears 1x, and IREN, Cipher and Bitdeer are below it.

Here both metrics use the same balance-sheet capital, so levels compare directly: on 9 Oct the market paid 3.18x EV / IC for 1.40x ROIC / WACC; on 25 Nov, 1.38x for 1.12x. The growth premium has mostly gone.

3. ALL 13

- ROIC / WACC fell 2.5%, from 1.25x (2Q26) to 1.22x (3Q26).
- EV / IC fell 25%, from 6.75x at the 9 Oct close to 5.08x at the 25 Nov close.

Yes, but this is the hyperscaler answer: neo-clouds are 0.5% of the 13's enterprise value at the 25 Nov close.

What we're watching 🔍

Oracle, which we hold, reports its November quarter on 14 Dec; its figures here are still from the quarter ended 31 August.

What would change our view: a 4Q26 hyperscaler ROIC / WACC reading falling as fast as EV / IC has.

item.description:
In the DRAM market, some Chinese CSPs began reducing their 2027 server DRAM bit demand outside long-term agreements (LTAs) in early 4Q26.
$DRAM
However, North American CSPs quickly absorbed the resulting supply availability, keeping overall DRAM bit demand on a strong growth trajectory for the year.

@SemiconductorsX：Chinese CSP order cuts are weighing on the 2027 memory price outlook. TrendForce lowered its NAND Flash revenue forecast to $419.3 billion and DRAM to $1.15 trillion.
$DRAM
Chinese cloud providers began cutting 2027 enterprise SSD plans in mid-fourth quarter amid GPU shortage concerns. Those reductions exceeded the extra orders from North American CSPs.

Low-cost memory inventories for PCs and smartphones are already depleted. Device prices face upward pressure next year. Brands are expected to cut NAND capacity specs to hold BOM costs. That slows NAND bit demand growth.

Supply keeps rising. Some makers expand capacity while others move to newer process nodes and raise bit output. The result is an oversupplied NAND market with lower contract prices. The revised $419.3 billion figure still shows 29% year-over-year growth.

On DRAM, some Chinese CSPs cut 2027 server bit demand outside long-term agreements in early fourth quarter. North American CSPs absorbed the freed supply, so overall bit demand stays on a strong growth path. Bit supply continues to rise as majors add wafer capacity and advance process nodes.

DRAM remains undersupplied through 2027. Quarterly contract price increases are expected to narrow and could level off in the second half. The revised $1.15 trillion forecast still represents 69% year-over-year growth.

item.title: @convequity：分析称华为计划于2027年2月推出自主HBM并加速Ascend 960DT芯片
item.description:
HBM is not Huawei's bottleneck. Its own memory stack has twice the data pins of HBM4

Huawei will present its own HBM, the stacked memory that feeds AI chips, at the ISSCC chip-design conference on 16 February 2027. The draft programme lists 4,096 data pins, twice the 2,048 of HBM4, the current standard. Its five layers are joined by wafer-on-wafer hybrid bonding, which bonds copper directly to copper with no solder.

Many investors still believe HBM is Huawei's bottleneck. Chosun Ilbo reported in September that CXMT, the Chinese memory maker, is stuck at a yield of about 25% on HBM3, where SK hynix is above 90%. The Information reported in November that smuggled Korean HBM often ends up with Huawei's customers.

In our view CXMT's low yield on standard HBM3 is a nothing burger. Huawei does not need to follow the HBM standard. It builds its own stack, with a wider interface, fewer layers and its own controllers inside, and it has no need to smuggle HBM.

So we are not surprised that Huawei is speeding up its Ascend 960DT AI chip, now due in 1Q27 instead of 4Q27. Our estimate from published specs: the 960DT moves 9.6 TB/s in and out of memory for 4 PFLOPS of compute. Nvidia's ($NVDA) Rubin moves 22 TB/s for 35 PFLOPS. Each Huawei chip has far less compute, but per unit of compute it has about 3.8x Rubin's memory bandwidth. The gap in networking bandwidth is wider.

We wrote in September 2025: "by using custom HBM standard whilst NVDA only customize the base die of HBM4, Huawei is ahead."

Huawei's progress is also great news for BE Semiconductor ($BESI), the Dutch maker of hybrid bonding machines and one of our holdings. Investors sold BESI this year because the HBM makers put hybrid bonding off and stayed on solder. It closed on 24 November 56% below its June high. Huawei's ISSCC papers put hybrid bonding in both memory and logic. If chipmakers outside China stay on solder, Huawei will outcompete them in both, so we expect them to adopt it. Seoul Economic Daily reported on 20 November that SK hynix plans to order BESI's hybrid bonders. We bought the dip in October.

Subscribers have the bonding mechanism in Huawei After Sanctions and our BESI position in the 4Q26 Portfolio Rebalance.

item.title: @convequity：亚马逊拟以约75亿美元收购Decart优化栈及团队，以增强Trainium芯片软件适配能力
item.description:
Amazon's Decart deal buys the chip-tuning work most Trainium customers cannot do themselves

Amazon ($AMZN) is buying the Decart Optimization Stack and hiring Decart's founders and team. The price is about $7.5B, a figure Amazon has not disclosed, and Decart's video models are not part of the deal. Anthropic ($ANT) walked away from buying Decart for about $6B in September. The stack is the software between an AI model and a chip. It tunes the kernels (the low-level routines that run a model's math on a given chip), the compiler and the runtime so more of the chip does useful work.

Decart stands out in two ways. It has done this on Trainium, Amazon's own AI chip, in Amazon's kernel language, as well as on Nvidia ($NVDA) and Google ($GOOGL) chips. And it redesigns the model to fit the chip: Decart said in December 2025 that it fused the three parts of its model, which normally run in sequence, into one program that runs them all at once on a Trainium chip.

Amazon is preparing to sell Trainium chips to customers. Each customer model needs kernels tuned for Trainium, and in our view most customers have no engineers who can write them. The founders must stay at Amazon for five years to be paid in full, terms Amazon has not confirmed, so the deal is built to keep the team.

Do AI-written kernels make this unnecessary? For frontier labs, increasingly yes. For Amazon, not yet.

Anthropic said in its IPO roadshow that its Mythos model got Claude running on AMD ($AMD) chips in three days and "ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels". OpenAI says AI-written versions of selected model blocks ran 1.5 to 1.8 times faster than its experts' versions.

Two limits remain. Checking: in the KernelBench-Verified study (August 2026), no model's kernels beat standard PyTorch code on average once the tests were tightened. New chips: in AWS's own Trainium benchmark (July 2026), Claude Opus 4.8 with no tools solved 6% of 150 kernel tasks. In a compile-and-test loop on a real chip, 83% compiled. Neither figure measures speed.

In our view the kernel code loses value as models improve. What lasts is deciding what to optimize, building the checks and redesigning the model for each new chip. The team does that work, which fits a payout tied to a five-year stay.

Broadcom ($AVGO) has bought no kernel or compiler company and has less reason to. Its custom-chip customers own their models and software: OpenAI says it optimized the chip it developed with Broadcom "around the kernels". The buyers of such teams, Nvidia and now Amazon, sell the same chips to many customers and must supply the software too. We think Broadcom would buy one only if it started selling a standard chip of its own to customers without kernel engineers.

item.title: @convequity：分析对比谷歌核电协议与SpaceX天然气轮机成本，指出天然气发电建设成本及速度优势
item.description:
Google's nuclear deal costs about $4.8B per GW to build. We estimate SpaceX's gas turbines at about $0.8B per GW

Constellation is spending more than $4.3B to raise the output of 11 reactors it already runs by 890 MW, and will sell that power to Google ($GOOGL) for 20 years. That is about $4.8B per GW, paid once by Constellation. Google's price is private. At the $85–115 per MWh analysts estimate for similar contracts, we estimate its bill at $0.7–0.9B per GW a year.

The first of the 890 MW is due by 2028 and the last before the end of 2032. The three big nuclear deals signed this year in PJM, the largest US power market, total 6,889 MW. Only 1,513 MW of that is new capacity.

SpaceX ($SPCX) runs its Colossus data centres largely on on-site gas turbines. A joint venture between Solaris and an xAI affiliate is buying about 900 MW of them. Its loan terms imply about $0.7B of spending, or about $0.8B per GW for generators and emissions controls, before fuel. A complete new gas plant costs about $2.4B per GW.

SpaceX is also faster. It ended September with 1.7 GW of compute capacity and expects 2.5–3 GW by the end of December. That is 0.8–1.3 GW added in one quarter, against 0.89 GW from the reactor upgrades for Google by 2032.

Our view: Google's new nuclear power costs two to six times more to build than gas power like SpaceX's and arrives years later. Gas has a fuel bill that nuclear largely avoids, so the gap is in building cost and speed. Our SpaceX report projects about $0.7B per GW to launch and power compute in orbit, if Starship reaches full reuse.

item.description:
InnoLight's customers are already giving 2028 demand guidance

InnoLight makes the optical transceivers that carry data between AI servers and switches inside data centres. This month it said some key customers have already given clear demand guidance for 2028.

What InnoLight has disclosed, in date order:
• 27 Apr: customers had given demand guidance for 2026 and 2027, and some key customers were planning their 2028 demand.
• 3 Nov, investor-relations record: the vast majority of 2027 orders already cover the full year.
• Same record: at least one key customer has given clear 2028 demand guidance, and that demand is strong. Guidance from other customers is still being collected.
• Same record: most customers have not cut demand or orders, and some have raised their demand for 1.6T modules, the fastest generation now shipping in volume. InnoLight published the record to answer rumours of overseas order cuts.
• 6 Nov, company announcement: major customers' orders largely cover all of 2027, and some key customers have given clear 2028 guidance.
• 18 Nov: to secure key materials, InnoLight is stocking early, signing long-term supply agreements and prepaying suppliers.
• First nine months of 2026: revenue of RMB 69.5 billion, up 178% on a year earlier, and net profit of RMB 22.2 billion, up 212%.

The 2028 guidance has come unusually early. Customers normally give a supplier next year's demand around the middle of the current year. On that schedule, 2028 guidance would arrive in mid-2027. InnoLight has it in November 2026, about half a year early.

Eoptolink, another large Chinese module maker, points the same way. In an 18 Nov announcement it said customer demand guidance is clear, orders in hand are ample, and it sees no downward revisions or order cuts.

A customer that guides this far ahead is, in our view, trying to secure supply. InnoLight said on 3 Nov that module supply is still tight. We read the 2028 guidance as evidence that demand for AI optics is strong and still building into 2027 and 2028.

item.title: @convequity：内存价格暴涨带动台积电及二线晶圆代工厂上调2027年报价，产能利用率接近饱和
item.description:
Memory prices rose more than fivefold in a year. Foundries are asking for 10% to more than 20% in 2027, and we think they have more room left.

Taiwanese chip designers have received foundry price notices of 10% to more than 20% for the first quarter of 2027. TSMC's own rise is smaller: 3% to 6% on wafers from January, highest on 2nm and 3nm.

Memory moved on a different scale. A 16Gb DDR5 chip cost about $8.70 on contract in October 2025 and $48 in September 2026, according to Team Group's CEO. That is 5.5 times in 11 months. Intel's CEO said in September that memory prices "have gone up five, six, and seven times". Counterpoint puts third-quarter DRAM revenue near $200 billion, close to five times a year earlier.

We think the slower pace helps the foundries. A chip buyer that has paid five times more for memory can pay 10% more for wafers, so foundries can keep raising prices in steps. Their revenue and profit should also be steadier. Part of memory is already turning down: TrendForce expects NAND flash contract prices to be flat to 5% lower in the first quarter of 2027.

The second-tier foundries are where the price rises spread next. They make older-generation chips and had spare capacity earlier this year. Most of it is now in use. UMC ($UMC) ran at 85% of capacity in the second quarter and 92% in the third. GlobalFoundries ($GFS) is in the high 80s, Vanguard is at about 90% and SMIC at 97%.

Their prices are following. UMC expects its average selling price to rise about 10% in 2027 and says shipment growth will be limited by capacity. GlobalFoundries reported its first year-on-year price rise since 2023 in the third quarter and expects about a 10% lift from price and product mix in 2027. Powerchip is negotiating rises of 10% to 20%.

A 10% rise is large for these companies. UMC's gross margin is 34%. If its costs stayed flat, a 10% price rise would lift that to about 40%. UMC says part of the rise covers its own higher costs, so the real gain will be smaller.

The risk is spare capacity coming back. GlobalFoundries went more than two years without a year-on-year price rise before the third quarter. Second-tier price rises last only while these fabs stay close to full.

item.title: @convequity：分析认为3D DRAM芯片设计面临散热与可靠性结构性限制，代工厂与制造集成成关键
item.description:
For investors looking at 3D DRAM chip designers such as d-Matrix and Fractile, the hard problems left are heat and reliability, and the company that designs the chip does not control the fix. We think that puts a structural ceiling on how far a fabless designer like Fractile can set its 3D DRAM apart.

d-Matrix has shown publicly how a designer can work around the heat. Fractile, a private fabless startup working on 3D DRAM, has not shown comparable work publicly.

3D DRAM means stacking memory directly on the compute chip. The connections between the two layers are mostly solved. Heat and reliability are not.

DRAM loses its data faster as it gets hotter. As temperature rises, each cell holds its data for a shorter time, so the memory has to be refreshed more often, and error rates climb.

A high-power logic die is the hottest part of the system. Put DRAM on it and the memory sits in the worst thermal spot there is. Heat from compute has to pass through the memory stack, or around it, to reach the cooler.

The fixes are process and packaging work: bonding materials, thermal paths, DRAM cells built for high temperatures, and test and yield at the level of the whole stack. That work belongs to the foundry and the memory maker.

A fabless designer, a company that designs chips and has someone else manufacture them, can do less. It can keep hot compute blocks away from sensitive memory banks, throttle, add error correction, or refresh more aggressively. These steps work around the physics, but a designer cannot change it.

d-Matrix is the reference case. It flips the stack and puts the compute die on top of the DRAM, so the cold plate sits directly on the hottest silicon and heat does not have to pass through the memory. That is useful engineering.

The other route is vertical integration. Huawei controls or tightly couples process, packaging and design, so it can tune the memory cell, the bond and the logic floorplan together. A fabless startup cannot.

That is why we see the ceiling as structural, and it limits what differentiation can mean for a company like Fractile. What we watch is whether Fractile shows public thermal and reliability work comparable to what d-Matrix has shown.

item.title: @convequity：AI内存需求转向速度：HBM堆叠层数增加如何影响数据传输与处理器性能
item.description:
For investors in AI memory: demand is moving toward speed, and a taller HBM stack only adds capacity. AI inference that answers quickly now commands a premium, and the memory speed it depends on is set by the stack's external interface.

An HBM stack is several layers of DRAM memory on a base die. The base die is a logic die that handles input and output, control and everything else that is not storage. In a conventional package, the base die talks to the processor through a silicon interposer.

Think of that package as a residential tower next to a one-storey office where the residents work. The HBM stack is the tower, the processor is the office, and the interposer is an underground passage between them.

To get to work, residents ride the elevators down. The elevators are TSVs, the vertical connections that run down through the stacked memory dies. There are about 12,000 of them across a 12-high stack.

At the bottom, the residents squeeze through a few exit gates, which are the stack's 2,048 pins, and then cross the passage.

Adding floors houses more residents, but they all still leave through the same few gates. Stacking more memory dies works the same way. Capacity goes up, and the external interface's width and signalling speed decide how much data reaches the processor.

Stack the memory directly above the logic and the residents live above their workplace. Elevators spread across the building drop them right next to the desks they need, with no shared exit and no trip next door.

In silicon, dense vertical connections give many more parallel paths between memory and logic over shorter wires. That also cuts the energy spent moving data.

Our view is that a taller HBM stack should be read as more capacity, and that the interface is where to look for how fast data reaches the processor.

item.title: @convequity：郭明錤称谷歌削减2027年博通TPU订单，市场反应与潜在影响分析
item.description:
Ming-Chi Kuo says Google cut 1 million Broadcom TPUs for 2027. I doubt those chips go unsold.

Kuo's 20 November supply-chain survey says Google cut 2027 shipments of the Broadcom-designed TPU 8i by about 1 million units, roughly 20%, mostly the higher-priced 8i Max, and will take more of MediaTek's TPU 8t. Broadcom ($AVGO) fell about 12% that day and lost about $200 billion of market value, in a session when the whole chip sector sold off. Neither company has commented.

I would treat the check with caution. Supply-chain checks from Taiwan tend to favor Taiwanese vendors, and checks on the US side tend to favor US vendors. The truth usually sits between the two.

Suppose the cut is real. At about $5,500–6,000 per TPU 8i, a price from a single expert call, 1 million units is about $5.5–6 billion of 2027 revenue. The 8i Max costs more, so the true figure would be higher. The market value lost that day was still more than 30 times that revenue.

The capacity would not sit idle either. AI chips are still short, and Kuo's own post cites a tight supply chain. Broadcom's CEO Hock Tan said in September that Broadcom expects Anthropic to deploy 5 GW of TPU 8i in 2027, meaning 5 gigawatts of data center power filled with these chips, with another 10 GW in view for 2028. Kuo's 16 November note put about 14 million Broadcom-designed 8i units with Anthropic across 2028 and 2029. If Google takes fewer chips, Broadcom has wafers and packaging slots to give to customers already waiting.

I also find Kuo's reason hard to follow. He says frontier model development gets first call on Google's compute. A growing part of that development is reinforcement learning after the main training run, where the model produces large volumes of output and is graded on it. That is inference work, the job the 8i was built for.

The risk is power. If Anthropic and other buyers cannot get data center power in 2027, the freed chips slip into 2028. Even so, I read the selloff as a better chance to buy Broadcom than a reason to sell it.
